back: Last minute changes are made under time pressure and are less likely to have been coordinated across every affected sheet, so they carry a higher risk of introducing a new inconsistency. Targeting recently revised sheets for extra scrutiny is an efficient way to focus limited QC time.

front: What is the purpose of a pre-issuance QC review focused specifically on drawing titles, scales, and sheet indexes?
back: It confirms that every sheet listed in the index actually exists in the issued set, that each sheet's title matches its content, and that stated scales are correct for how the drawing will be printed. Missing this check can leave a contractor working from an incomplete or mislabeled set.

front: Why should a QC reviewer confirm that a recently issued addendum or bulletin has been incorporated consistently across all affected sheets?
back: A change issued in an addendum is sometimes applied to the plan sheet where the change originated but missed on a related detail, schedule, or section elsewhere in the set. Checking that the change was carried through everywhere it applies prevents the set from contradicting its own addendum.

front: What is the benefit of running a project QC checkpoint immediately before a design is presented to the owner, separate from the milestone checkpoints?
back: A pre-presentation checkpoint catches embarrassing or confidence damaging errors, such as an outdated image or an unresolved conflict, before the owner sees the material. It protects the firm's credibility even when the underlying technical content will still be refined further before the next formal milestone.

front: Why is verifying consistent units of measurement, such as feet and inches versus decimal feet, part of document QC?
back: Mixed unit formats across a set, or between the architectural and civil drawings, increase the chance of a contractor misreading a dimension. Standardizing and verifying the unit format used throughout the set removes an avoidable source of field error.

front: What is the purpose of checking that a project's drawing set uses consistent line weights and graphic standards across sheets produced by different team members?
back: Inconsistent line weights or hatching between sheets drafted by different staff can make a set harder to read and can obscure the distinction between new work, existing work, and demolition. A QC review confirms the set reads as one coordinated document rather than a patchwork of individual styles.

front: Why should a QC reviewer check that demolition plans and new construction plans agree on what is being removed versus retained?
back: An item shown to be demolished on one sheet but shown as existing to remain on another creates a direct contradiction that a contractor cannot resolve without an RFI. Confirming demolition scope is consistent across all affected sheets is a key check on renovation projects.

front: What is the purpose of a QC checkpoint that compares the drawing set against the owner's approved program document?
back: It confirms that required spaces, adjacencies, and area targets from the approved program are still reflected in the current design, since design development can drift from the original program without anyone deliberately deciding to change it. Catching that drift early avoids delivering a design the owner did not actually approve.

front: Why should a project QC process include a check that consultant drawings received from outside disciplines have been reviewed before incorporation into the coordinated set?
back: A consultant's drawings can contain the same kinds of errors as the architect's own work, and simply inserting them into the set without review risks propagating those errors into the coordinated document. The architect remains responsible for confirming consultant work is coordinated with the rest of the set.

front: What is the purpose of documenting QC review comments in a way that distinguishes required corrections from optional suggestions?
back: Mixing a mandatory correction with a stylistic suggestion in the same undifferentiated markup makes it harder for the drafting team to prioritize what must be fixed before issuance. Clearly separating the two ensures required items are never mistaken for something that can be skipped under deadline pressure.

front: Overall, why is project level QA/QC considered a cost control tool as well as a quality tool?
back: Errors caught in the office during design cost only staff time to fix, while the same errors discovered during construction can trigger change orders, delay claims, and rework that far exceed the cost of the original design effort. Project QA/QC therefore protects the project's budget and schedule, not only the technical accuracy of the documents.

front: Why must the code data plate or code analysis diagram be re-verified at every QC checkpoint, not just once?
back: The code analysis summarizes occupancy classification, construction type, occupant load, and egress requirements based on the design as it exists at that moment. As the design evolves through SD, DD, and CD, changes elsewhere in the project can invalidate an earlier code analysis, so it must be checked against the current drawings at every milestone.

front: What does a QC reviewer check when verifying an occupant load calculation?
back: The reviewer confirms the correct occupancy-specific area factor, net or gross as required by the code, has been applied to the actual area of each space, and that the resulting occupant load is used consistently throughout the egress analysis. An incorrect factor understates the true occupant load and can lead to undersized exits.

front: How does a QC checkpoint verify that an egress component, such as a corridor or stairway, is wide enough?
back: The code assigns a capacity factor, expressed in inches of width per occupant, and stairways generally require a larger factor than other components such as doors and corridors. The reviewer multiplies the occupant load that component serves by the applicable factor and confirms the drawn width meets or exceeds that result.

front: What is verified in a travel distance check during project QC?
back: The reviewer measures the actual path of travel from the most remote point in a space to the nearest exit and confirms it does not exceed the maximum allowed for that occupancy classification and sprinkler condition. This measurement must be redone whenever partitions, furniture layouts, or exit locations change.

front: What is a common path of travel, and why does QC review check its length?
back: A common path of travel is the portion of an egress route where occupants have only one direction of travel before reaching a point where two separate paths to two exits become available. The code limits how long this single path can be, so QC review confirms the layout provides two distinct paths within that limit.

front: What does a dead-end corridor check verify?
back: It confirms that any corridor segment leading to a dead end, with no path through to an exit, does not exceed the maximum length the code allows for that occupancy and sprinkler condition. An oversized dead end forces occupants to backtrack toward a fire or hazard rather than away from it.

front: What triggers a QC reviewer to check whether a space has enough required exits?
back: The code sets occupant load thresholds above which a room, story, or building must be provided with two, three, or more separate exits rather than just one. A QC reviewer compares the calculated occupant load against these thresholds and confirms the plan actually shows the required number of exits.

front: What is fire separation distance, and why does QC review check it?
back: Fire separation distance is the distance from an exterior wall to the property line, an assumed property line, or another building on the same lot. It governs how much unprotected wall opening is allowed and whether the exterior wall itself must carry a fire-resistance rating, so QC review confirms the drawn distance and the wall design agree with each other.

front: What does a QC checkpoint confirm about allowable building area and height?
back: The code sets a maximum allowable floor area and building height based on the construction type and occupancy classification, with increases often available for sprinkler protection or open frontage. The reviewer confirms the actual building as designed still falls within the allowance calculated for its assigned construction type.

front: What is checked when verifying corridor fire-resistance ratings during QC review?
back: The reviewer confirms corridors serving a given occupancy and occupant load carry the fire-resistance rating the code requires, which can depend on whether the building is sprinklered. A corridor shown without the required rating, or built to a rating lower than what its wall assembly detail achieves, is a life safety defect.

front: What does QC review check regarding penetrations through fire-rated assemblies?
back: Any duct, pipe, or conduit passing through a rated wall or floor must be sealed with a tested and listed firestop system, and ducts penetrating rated assemblies typically require a fire damper or smoke damper. QC review confirms these penetration details are shown and that the assumed rating of the assembly is not compromised by an unprotected opening.

front: Why does QC review confirm the listed assembly number referenced on a rated wall detail?
back: A fire-resistance rating is only valid if the wall is built exactly as tested, so the reviewer confirms the referenced listing number corresponds to an assembly that actually matches the materials and layer thicknesses shown in the detail. Substituting a different stud gauge, insulation, or board thickness without checking the listing can invalidate the claimed rating.

front: What does an accessible route verification check during document QC?
back: It confirms there is a continuous, unobstructed path meeting slope, width, and surface requirements connecting the accessible parking and site arrival points to the accessible building entrance. A gap in this route, such as a curb with no ramp, is a common finding caught only by walking the route on the plan step by step.

front: What does QC review check about accessible parking spaces?
back: The reviewer confirms the number of accessible spaces shown matches what is required based on the total parking count, and that the required proportion of those spaces is designated van accessible with the correct additional width or access aisle. This count must be rechecked whenever the total number of parking spaces changes.

front: What does a plumbing fixture count check verify during project QC?
back: It confirms the number of water closets, lavatories, and other required fixtures shown on the plans meets the plumbing code's minimum count for that occupancy classification and occupant load, typically split by sex where the code requires. An undercount discovered late can require adding entire toilet rooms after layouts are otherwise finalized.

front: Why does QC review check the swing direction of certain doors along the egress path?
back: Doors serving a room or space with an occupant load at or above a threshold set by the code must swing in the direction of egress travel so they cannot be blocked by a crowd moving toward them. A reviewer checks each door tag against its room's occupant load to confirm the swing direction shown is correct.

front: When does QC review flag a door as requiring panic hardware?
back: Doors serving assembly and educational occupancies with occupant loads above the threshold set by the code, and doors to rooms containing certain hazardous materials, must be equipped with panic or fire exit hardware rather than a standard latch. A reviewer cross-checks the door hardware schedule against these occupant load and use conditions.

front: What does QC review check about stair riser and tread dimensions?
back: The reviewer confirms riser heights and tread depths fall within the code's minimum and maximum limits and that the variation between the largest and smallest riser or tread within a single flight stays within the code's tight tolerance. An inconsistent riser height within a flight is a common trip hazard the code specifically limits.

front: What is checked when verifying guard and handrail heights during QC review?
back: Guards protecting a walking surface with a drop-off typically must reach a minimum height around 42 inches, while handrails on stairs are held to a narrower height range, commonly around 34 to 38 inches. The reviewer confirms the dimensions shown in section details match these requirements rather than an arbitrary design height.

front: What does a safety glazing check verify in hazardous locations?
back: It confirms that glazing in doors, in sidelites near doors, and in wet areas such as tubs and showers is specified as tempered or laminated safety glazing rather than standard annealed glass. A missed safety glazing callout in one of these locations is both a code violation and a real injury risk.

front: What does QC review check regarding fire alarm and sprinkler system requirements?
back: The reviewer confirms whether the building's occupancy classification, area, or height triggers a mandatory fire alarm or automatic sprinkler system under the code, and that the drawings and code analysis agree on which systems are actually required. Assuming sprinklers when they are not actually required, or vice versa, invalidates every allowance in the code analysis that depends on that assumption.

front: What is a smoke compartment check, and on which occupancy does it typically apply?
back: Institutional occupancies such as hospitals and nursing homes must be subdivided into smoke compartments below a maximum allowable area, each with access to at least two means of egress. QC review confirms the smoke barrier locations shown on the plan actually create compartments within the code's area limit.

front: How does zoning compliance verification differ from building code compliance verification in project QC?
back: Zoning compliance checks site-level requirements set by the local zoning ordinance, such as setbacks, maximum height, and floor area ratio, while building code compliance checks life safety and construction requirements set by the adopted building code. Both must be verified separately, since a design can satisfy one and still violate the other.

front: What does QC review check about accessible clear floor space at plumbing fixtures?
back: It confirms the clearances and reach ranges around fixtures such as water closets and lavatories in accessible toilet rooms meet the minimum dimensions set by the applicable accessibility standard. A fixture shown too close to an adjacent wall or partition can make a room fail an accessibility inspection even if every other requirement is met.

front: What does a QC checkpoint verify about egress illumination and exit signage?
back: It confirms exit signs are shown at every location the code requires along the egress path, and that means of egress illumination, including any required emergency power backup, is documented on the electrical drawings. Missing signage or illumination at a single stair landing is a common finding in a life safety coordination review.

front: Why does a dedicated code compliance checkpoint happen immediately before permit submission?
back: This checkpoint is the last internal chance to catch a code deficiency before the drawings are reviewed by the authority having jurisdiction. Correcting a plan review comment after submission delays the permit and the entire project schedule, so this final internal check aims to reduce the number of comments the reviewing jurisdiction sends back.

front: What does a QC checkpoint verify about the fire-resistance rating of the structural frame?
back: It confirms the fire-resistance rating shown for columns, beams, and floor or roof assemblies matches what the code requires for the building's assigned construction type. If the construction type assumption changes during design, every structural member's required rating must be rechecked against the new requirement.

front: Why must the life safety or code plan sheet be checked against the current architectural floor plan at every issuance?
back: The life safety plan is often produced once early in the project and then not actively updated as the architectural plan changes through later phases. QC review compares wall locations, door locations, and rated separations on the life safety plan against the current architectural plan to catch drift between the two.

front: Why does QC review confirm the sprinklered status assumed in the code analysis still matches the actual design?
back: Many code allowances, such as increased travel distance, reduced corridor rating, or increased allowable area, depend on the building being fully sprinklered. If a later design change removes sprinkler coverage from part of the building without updating the code analysis, every allowance based on that assumption becomes invalid.

front: What is the 1:10:100 rule as applied to the cost of catching a design error?
back: It is a general quality management principle stating that preventing an error costs roughly one unit, correcting it internally before it leaves the office costs roughly ten times as much, and correcting it after it reaches the field costs roughly one hundred times as much. The rule illustrates why front-loaded QA/QC effort is far cheaper than fixing problems discovered during construction.

front: In the cost of quality framework, what are prevention costs?
back: Prevention costs are the resources spent to keep errors from occurring in the first place, such as staff training, standardized checklists, and established QC procedures for every project. Money spent on prevention is generally the least expensive category in the cost of quality framework.

front: In the cost of quality framework, what are appraisal costs?
back: Appraisal costs are the resources spent to find errors that still occurred despite prevention efforts, such as peer review, redline markup review, and code compliance checkpoints. These costs are incurred before the documents are issued, so they are still relatively inexpensive compared to fixing an error that was never found internally.

front: In the cost of quality framework, what is an internal failure cost?
back: An internal failure cost is the cost of correcting an error that was caught before the documents left the firm, such as revising a set based on a redline before it is issued for permit or bid. It is more expensive than a prevention or appraisal cost, but far less expensive than the same error being caught after issuance.

front: In the cost of quality framework, what is an external failure cost, and why is it the most expensive category?
back: An external failure cost is the cost of an error not caught until after the documents were relied on by the client or contractor, resulting in change orders, RFIs, claims, or rework in the field. It is the most expensive category because it can add contractor markup, demolition of installed work, and schedule delay on top of the correction itself.

front: What does the MacLeamy curve illustrate about the timing of design effort and project QC?
back: It shows that the ability to influence a project's cost and functional outcomes is greatest early in design and decreases steadily as the project proceeds, while the cost of making a design change moves in the opposite direction, rising steeply later on. The curve is used to argue for front-loading design effort and QC checkpoints into the earliest phases rather than concentrating review at the end.

front: Why does an identical design change typically cost more to implement during Construction Documents than during Schematic Design?
back: By CD phase, structural, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing drawings have all been developed around the original decision, so a change ripples across every affected discipline's sheets rather than a single concept sketch. Making the same change earlier avoids the coordinated rework across multiple drawing sets that a late change requires.

front: What cost components does a formal construction change order add on top of simply correcting an error?
back: A change order typically adds the contractor's markup for overhead and profit, potential general conditions cost for extended time on site, and possible schedule impact or liquidated damages exposure. None of these added costs apply when the same error is caught and corrected on paper before the documents are issued.

front: Why does demolition of already-installed work make a field-discovered error especially costly?
back: Once work has been built, correcting a design error often requires removing and disposing of the installed material before the corrected work can be rebuilt, adding demolition labor and material waste on top of the original construction cost. A paper correction avoids this entirely, since nothing physical has been built yet.

front: How does an uncaught QC error connect to an architect's professional liability exposure?
back: An error that reaches construction and causes cost overrun, delay, or physical damage can expose the firm to a claim against its errors and omissions insurance. Project QA/QC is therefore a risk management function as well as a technical quality function, since it reduces the number of errors that could ever become a claim.

front: Why is an internal failure cost cheaper than an external failure cost for the same underlying error?
back: An internal failure is caught and corrected while the documents are still under the firm's control, requiring only staff time to revise a drawing. An external failure is caught after the client or contractor has already relied on the documents, adding contractor markup, possible rework of installed work, and schedule and liability exposure that an internal correction never triggers.

front: How does the cost of correcting an error generally change across a project's timeline, from early design through construction?
back: The cost stays relatively low and flat during early design phases, then rises through Construction Documents, and rises most steeply once construction has begun. This shape is the basis for scheduling QC checkpoints as early and as frequently as possible rather than relying on a single review near the end.

front: What does a sheet index verification check confirm before a set is issued?
back: It confirms every sheet listed in the index is actually included in the issued set, and every sheet actually included is listed in the index. A missing sheet or an orphaned index entry can mean the contractor is bidding or building from an incomplete set without realizing it.

front: Why does QC review check north arrow orientation across a drawing set?
back: It confirms the north arrow is shown at a consistent orientation across architectural, structural, civil, and landscape plan sheets, or, if a sheet is intentionally rotated for readability, that the rotation is clearly noted. An inconsistent or missing north arrow can cause disciplines reviewing the set together to misread how the drawings relate to each other.

front: What does an abbreviations legend check verify?
back: It confirms every abbreviation used anywhere in the drawing set actually appears in the abbreviations legend with the correct meaning, and flags any legend entry that is never actually used on the drawings. An undefined abbreviation forces the contractor to guess its meaning.

front: What does a symbols legend check verify during document QC?
back: It confirms every graphic symbol used on the plans, such as wall type tags, door tags, and window tags, has a matching entry in the symbols legend with the correct meaning. A symbol used on a plan but left undefined in the legend leaves the contractor unable to confirm what that element actually is.

front: What does a title block consistency check verify across a drawing set?
back: It confirms the project name, address, phase such as SD, DD, or CD, and the current issue date are correct and consistent on every sheet's title block. An outdated or mismatched title block on even one sheet can cause confusion about which version of the set is the authoritative one.

front: What does QC review check when comparing structural general notes to the structural calculations?
back: It confirms the design criteria stated in the general notes, such as live loads, wind loads, and seismic design category, match the assumptions actually used in the calculations. A mismatch here means either the notes on the drawings or the calculations themselves are wrong, and the discrepancy must be resolved before issuance.

front: What does QC review check regarding specification section numbering and drawing callouts?
back: It confirms specification sections are numbered correctly under the CSI MasterFormat system, and that every specification section referenced by a keynote or callout on the drawings actually exists in the project manual under that same number. A callout pointing to a nonexistent or renumbered section leaves the contractor unable to find the required requirements.

front: Why does QC review confirm that addenda or bulletins have been incorporated into the base drawing set before the next milestone?
back: Changes issued through an addendum or bulletin during a prior phase can otherwise remain only in that separate document while the base drawing set continues to show the original, superseded condition. Confirming incorporation before the next issuance prevents two conflicting descriptions of the same condition from existing side by side in the project record.

front: Why does QC review check that grid lines and key dimensions agree between the civil site plan and the architectural building footprint?
back: The civil site plan establishes the building's location relative to property lines and site features, and the architectural plan establishes the building's own internal grid and dimensions. A mismatch between the two can place the building in the wrong location on site even when each drawing is internally correct on its own.

front: Why does QC review check furniture and equipment plans against structural and MEP drawings?
back: Furniture and equipment plans are often produced separately and later in the process, so a workstation or equipment item can end up shown directly on top of a structural column, shear wall, or an MEP element such as a diffuser or electrical panel. QC review overlays these plans to catch conflicts before they reach the client or contractor.

front: What is a constructability review, and what does it add to project QC that a purely technical review does not?
back: A constructability review brings contractor or estimator input into the QC process before documents are issued, checking whether the details shown can actually be built as drawn, in a reasonable sequence, and within the assumed cost. A design-focused technical review can confirm a detail is code compliant and internally consistent without necessarily confirming it is practical to build.

front: What are the main types of reviews a project may undergo as part of project level QA/QC?
back: A technical review checks accuracy and cross-discipline coordination, a code review checks compliance with applicable codes, a cost review checks that the design still aligns with the project budget, and a constructability review checks whether the design can actually be built as documented. A single reviewer or checkpoint does not necessarily cover all four.

front: Why does QC review check that dimensions throughout a drawing are measured from a single consistent datum?
back: Mixing reference points, such as dimensioning some walls from column grid lines and others from a face of wall with no clear tie back to the grid, makes it easy for small errors to compound without being noticed. Confirming a single consistent datum is used throughout a sheet lets a reviewer trust that a dimension string will actually add up correctly.

front: What is a drawing issue log, and what role does it play in project QC?
back: A drawing issue log tracks every version of the drawing set issued for a specific purpose, such as permit, bid, or construction, along with its issue date and revision status. It lets the QC process confirm which set is the current, authoritative one and helps prevent a team member or contractor from working off a superseded version.

front: Microclimate
back: The distinct climate conditions of a small, specific area (a site or part of a site) that differ from the broader regional climate due to factors like topography, vegetation, water bodies, and surrounding buildings.

front: Solar access
back: The ability of a site or building to receive direct sunlight without obstruction from neighboring structures, terrain, or vegetation. Solar access studies inform siting for passive solar heating and photovoltaic potential.

front: Passive solar design, five basic elements
back: Aperture (south-facing glazing to admit sun), absorber (a hard, darkened surface that absorbs solar radiation), thermal mass (material to store that heat, such as concrete or masonry), distribution (how stored heat reaches occupied spaces, often by conduction, convection, or radiation), and control (overhangs, shading devices, and vents used to regulate how much heat is admitted or released).

front: Best building orientation for passive solar gain in the Northern Hemisphere
back: The building's long axis runs east-west, placing the greatest glazed area on the south facade to maximize winter sun exposure while minimizing low-angle east and west exposure.

front: Wind rose diagram
back: A graphic tool showing the frequency and speed of wind from different directions over a given period at a site, used to inform building orientation, natural ventilation strategies, and placement of outdoor spaces.

front: Prevailing wind
back: The direction from which wind most frequently blows at a given site over the course of a year or season, a key input for siting operable windows, courtyards, and windbreaks for natural ventilation and heat loss control.

front: Purpose of an early site inventory and analysis phase
back: To catalog existing physical, environmental, and contextual conditions (topography, vegetation, climate, views, utilities, neighborhood character) before design begins, so opportunities and constraints can shape siting decisions rather than being discovered later.

front: Alternative energy resources to evaluate during site analysis
back: Solar radiation for photovoltaics or solar thermal, wind for small-scale turbines, geothermal for ground-source heat pumps, and in some regions biomass, each with site-specific feasibility depending on exposure, land area, and geology.

front: Ground-source (geothermal) heat pump
back: A heating and cooling system that exchanges heat with the relatively stable temperature of the earth through buried pipe loops, reducing energy use compared to conventional systems but requiring adequate land area or well depth on the site.

front: Neighborhood context analysis
back: A study of the surrounding built and social environment, including adjacent building scale and use, street pattern, cultural landmarks, demographics, and community character, used to identify socio-cultural opportunities and constraints for a project.

front: Viewshed
back: The geographic area visible from a specific point or, conversely, the area from which a specific point or building can be seen. Viewshed analysis identifies valuable views to preserve or frame and negative views to screen.

front: Natural landscape features to document in site analysis
back: Existing vegetation, mature trees, water bodies, wetlands, rock outcroppings, and topographic variation, all of which can present both design opportunities (shade, habitat, character) and constraints on where a building may be placed.

front: Sun path diagram
back: A graphic representation of the sun's position in the sky (altitude and azimuth) at a given latitude across the day and year, used to predict shading patterns, daylight availability, and solar heat gain on a site.

front: Daylighting as a site opportunity
back: Designing to admit natural light deep into occupied spaces, reducing electric lighting loads and improving occupant well-being. Site orientation, adjacent obstructions, and reflective ground surfaces all affect daylighting potential.

front: Urban heat island effect
back: The tendency of dense urban areas with extensive paving and dark roofing to have significantly higher air temperatures than surrounding rural areas, a contextual condition that affects cooling loads, material selection, and landscape strategy.

front: 100-year floodplain
back: An area with a 1% chance of flooding in any given year, mapped by FEMA as the Special Flood Hazard Area. Development within it typically triggers flood insurance requirements and elevation or floodproofing standards.

front: Base Flood Elevation (BFE)
back: The computed elevation to which floodwater is anticipated to rise during the base (100-year) flood, shown on FEMA flood maps. Lowest floor elevations for new construction are typically set at or above the BFE, often plus freeboard.

front: FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM)
back: The official map produced by FEMA showing flood zones, base flood elevations, and floodway boundaries for a community, used during site analysis to determine flood risk and applicable building requirements.

front: Flood Zone A vs Zone AE
back: Zone A is a high-risk flood area where no base flood elevation has been determined. Zone AE is a high-risk area where the base flood elevation has been calculated and published, giving more precise design guidance.

front: Flood Zone V (coastal high hazard area)
back: A high-risk coastal flood zone subject to wave action in addition to inundation. Structures in Zone V generally must be elevated on pilings or columns with breakaway walls below the BFE, since flood barriers would not survive wave forces.

front: Freeboard
back: An additional margin of elevation, typically 1 to 2 feet, added above the base flood elevation as a safety factor when setting the lowest floor or mechanical equipment height, often required by local ordinance beyond the federal minimum.

front: Floodway vs flood fringe
back: The floodway is the channel and adjacent area that must remain clear to convey floodwater without significantly raising flood heights; new construction there is heavily restricted. The flood fringe is the outer area where water pools but development is more feasible with mitigation.

front: Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA)
back: The general term FEMA uses for land within the 100-year floodplain, encompassing Zones A, AE, and V. Its boundary is the trigger point for mandatory flood insurance and floodplain development regulations.

front: 50% substantial improvement rule
back: If the cost of renovating an existing structure in a floodplain equals or exceeds 50% of its market value, the entire structure must be brought into compliance with current floodplain construction standards, not just the renovated portion.

front: Dry floodproofing vs wet floodproofing
back: Dry floodproofing seals a structure to keep floodwater out entirely (used for non-residential buildings below the BFE in limited cases). Wet floodproofing allows floodwater to enter and exit an unoccupied lower level, using flood-resistant materials to minimize damage.

front: Geotechnical report
back: A study prepared by a geotechnical engineer describing subsurface soil and rock conditions, groundwater levels, and bearing capacity, used to inform foundation design, siting, and identification of soil-related hazards.

front: Expansive soil
back: Clay-rich soil that swells significantly when it absorbs moisture and shrinks when it dries, capable of exerting enough pressure to crack foundations and slabs. Mitigation includes deep foundations, moisture barriers, and controlled site drainage.

front: Liquefaction
back: A phenomenon in which saturated, loose granular soil temporarily loses strength and behaves like a liquid during strong ground shaking, most often from an earthquake, potentially causing foundations to sink or shift.

front: Soil bearing capacity
back: The maximum pressure that soil can support without excessive settlement or shear failure, expressed in pounds per square foot. It directly determines whether a shallow spread footing is feasible or a deep foundation system is required.

front: Subsidence
back: The gradual sinking or settling of the ground surface, often caused by groundwater extraction, mining, or organic soil decomposition, which can cause differential settlement and structural damage over time.

front: Karst topography
back: Terrain formed over soluble bedrock such as limestone, prone to sinkholes and underground voids. Sites in karst regions require specialized geotechnical investigation to locate voids before foundation design proceeds.

front: Percolation test
back: A field test that measures how quickly water drains through soil at a site, used primarily to size septic drain fields and inform stormwater infiltration design where soil absorption capacity matters.

front: Slope stability as a site constraint
back: Steep or unstable slopes are prone to erosion, landslides, or slippage, especially after saturation. Geotechnical analysis of slope stability determines buildable areas, required setbacks from slope edges, and retaining structure needs.

front: Radon
back: A naturally occurring, colorless, odorless radioactive gas produced by the decay of uranium in soil and rock. It enters buildings primarily through foundation cracks and gaps and is a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.

front: EPA radon zone map
back: A county-level map published by the EPA classifying areas into three zones by predicted average indoor radon potential, used during site analysis as a screening tool for whether radon testing and mitigation should be anticipated.

front: EPA radon action level
back: 4 picocuries per liter (pCi/L) of air. The EPA recommends mitigation when indoor radon testing results meet or exceed this level, though EPA notes there is no known safe threshold below it.

front: Sub-slab depressurization
back: The most common active radon mitigation method, using a fan and vent pipe system to draw radon gas from beneath a slab or foundation and exhaust it above the roofline before it can enter occupied space.

front: Radon-Resistant New Construction (RRNC)
back: A set of passive design and construction techniques, including a gas-permeable layer, sealed foundation penetrations, and a vent pipe stub, installed during new construction so a fan can be added later at low cost if testing shows elevated radon.

front: When to test for radon in a project timeline
back: Radon testing should occur early during site and building due diligence, and again after construction is complete and the building is closed up, since radon levels can change with construction and mechanical system operation.

front: Lead-based paint hazard
back: Paint containing lead, common in buildings constructed before 1978, that becomes hazardous when it deteriorates, is disturbed by renovation, or is present as dust and chips, posing serious neurological risk especially to children.

front: 1978 lead paint cutoff date
back: The year the United States banned residential use of lead-based paint. Any structure built before 1978 is presumed to contain lead-based paint unless testing proves otherwise, triggering specific disclosure and renovation requirements.

front: EPA Renovation, Repair, and Painting (RRP) Rule
back: A federal rule requiring contractors working on pre-1978 housing and child-occupied facilities to be lead-certified and to follow lead-safe work practices whenever their work disturbs more than a minimal area of painted surface.

front: Lead abatement vs interim controls
back: Abatement permanently eliminates a lead hazard, such as by removing or fully encapsulating painted components. Interim controls are temporary measures, such as repainting or repairing damaged surfaces, that reduce exposure but do not eliminate the hazard.

front: XRF testing
back: X-ray fluorescence testing, a common non-destructive method for detecting lead in paint on building components in place, used during renovation planning to identify which surfaces require lead-safe work practices.

front: Other common lead exposure pathways on a site
back: Beyond paint, lead can be present in contaminated soil near older structures or roadways and in drinking water from lead service lines or lead solder, both of which should be evaluated during environmental due diligence.

front: Brownfield
back: A property where redevelopment or reuse is complicated by the presence or potential presence of a hazardous substance, pollutant, or contaminant, often a former industrial or commercial site, as defined under federal brownfields law.

front: Phase I Environmental Site Assessment (ESA)
back: A non-invasive investigation of a property's historical use, records, and visual conditions to identify potential or existing environmental contamination, performed before purchase to establish liability protection and guide further study.

front: Phase II Environmental Site Assessment (ESA)
back: A follow-up investigation triggered when a Phase I identifies a recognized environmental condition, involving actual soil, groundwater, or material sampling and laboratory analysis to confirm and characterize contamination.

front: Recognized Environmental Condition (REC)
back: A Phase I ESA finding indicating the presence or likely presence of a hazardous substance or petroleum product on a property under conditions that suggest a release to the environment, requiring further investigation.

front: Common brownfield remediation methods
back: Excavation and off-site disposal of contaminated soil, capping to isolate contamination in place, and bioremediation using microorganisms to break down contaminants, chosen based on contaminant type, site conditions, and cost.

front: Institutional controls on a remediated site
back: Legal or administrative restrictions, such as deed restrictions limiting future land use or requiring maintenance of an engineered cap, put in place after remediation when contamination is managed rather than fully removed.

front: EPA Brownfields grant program
back: Federal funding administered by the EPA to help communities and developers assess, clean up, and reuse brownfield sites, often a key financial factor in the feasibility of redeveloping a contaminated property.

front: State voluntary cleanup program
back: A state-level program that allows a property owner or developer to remediate contamination under state oversight in exchange for liability protection, often faster and more flexible than federal Superfund processes.

front: Due diligence on an abandoned structure
back: Before design begins on a site with an abandoned building, the team should assess structural stability, hazardous materials, code compliance history, and demolition versus adaptive reuse feasibility as part of environmental and contextual analysis.

front: Asbestos-containing materials (ACM)
back: Building materials such as insulation, floor tile, and roofing that contain asbestos fibers, common in structures built before the 1980s. ACM is generally safe if undisturbed but hazardous when damaged or during renovation and demolition.

front: PCBs (polychlorinated biphenyls)
back: Toxic industrial compounds once common in electrical equipment, caulking, and fluorescent light ballasts, particularly in buildings constructed or renovated before 1979, requiring identification and special disposal during renovation or demolition.

front: Underground storage tank (UST)
back: A buried tank, often for fuel oil or gasoline, common on former gas station or industrial sites, that poses a soil and groundwater contamination risk if leaking. UST identification and removal is a standard part of environmental site assessment.

front: Sea level rise as a siting consideration
back: For coastal or waterfront sites, projected sea level rise over a building's service life should inform finished floor elevation, site grading, and long-term flood risk, beyond what current FEMA maps alone indicate.

front: Climate-change vulnerability assessment
back: An evaluation of how a site and building are likely to be affected over their service life by shifting climate conditions, including increased flooding, extreme heat, drought, or storm intensity, used to inform resilient siting and design decisions.

front: Mitigating urban heat island effect at the site level
back: Strategies include high-albedo or vegetated roofing, shade trees, permeable and light-colored paving, and reducing dark impervious surface area, all of which lower site and ambient temperatures compared to conventional paved development.

front: Wildland-urban interface (WUI)
back: The zone where development meets or intermingles with undeveloped wildland vegetation, carrying elevated wildfire risk. Siting and design in the WUI often require defensible space, fire-resistant materials, and ember-resistant vent details.

front: Resilient design
back: A design approach that anticipates and plans for disruptive events, whether natural hazards or climate-related stresses, so a building and site can continue functioning, be quickly repaired, or protect occupants when conditions exceed historical norms.

front: Storm intensification and historical flood data
back: Because climate trends are increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme precipitation events, relying solely on historical 100-year storm data may understate future flood risk, prompting many jurisdictions to require added freeboard or updated modeling.

front: Managed retreat
back: A climate adaptation strategy that involves relocating development away from high-risk coastal or floodplain areas over time, rather than continuing to armor or elevate structures in place, considered when long-term risk outweighs mitigation cost.

front: Passive survivability
back: A building's ability to maintain habitable interior conditions, such as safe temperature and air quality, during an extended utility outage, achieved through a well-insulated envelope, passive solar and shading strategies, and natural ventilation.

front: Minimizing building footprint as a sustainability strategy
back: Reducing a building's ground-level footprint preserves permeable land, existing vegetation, and habitat while lowering stormwater runoff and site disturbance, often achieved by building taller or more compactly rather than spreading horizontally.

front: Massing strategy for passive solar performance
back: An elongated east-west building form with the majority of glazing on the south facade maximizes winter solar heat gain while minimizing harder-to-shade east and west exposure, improving passive heating and daylighting performance.

front: Why east-west long axis orientation is preferred for solar performance
back: It exposes the largest facade area to the south, where the sun's path is easiest to control with fixed horizontal overhangs, while minimizing exposure to the low, hard-to-shade morning and afternoon sun from the east and west.

front: Fixed horizontal overhangs for solar shading
back: Overhangs sized using the sun's seasonal altitude angle can block high summer sun to reduce cooling loads while still admitting low winter sun for passive heating on south-facing glazing, a passive design strategy tied directly to orientation.

front: Window-to-wall ratio (WWR)
back: The proportion of a facade's area that is glazed versus opaque. WWR affects daylighting, views, heat gain, and heat loss, and is often tuned differently by orientation, with more glazing to the south and less to the east and west.

front: Thermal mass in passive design
back: Dense materials such as concrete, masonry, or tile that absorb heat during the day and release it slowly, helping moderate indoor temperature swings and store solar heat gain for release after the sun sets.

front: Passive cooling strategies driven by orientation
back: Cross ventilation uses operable openings on opposite facades aligned with prevailing breezes, while the stack effect uses vertical temperature and pressure differences to draw warm air out through high openings, both reducing reliance on mechanical cooling.

front: Infill site vs greenfield site
back: An infill site is an underused or vacant parcel within an already developed area, typically favored for sustainability since it reuses existing infrastructure. A greenfield site is previously undeveloped land, often requiring new infrastructure and disturbing more natural systems.

front: LEED Sustainable Sites category, general intent
back: Encourages site selection and design decisions that protect ecologically sensitive land, reduce site disturbance, manage stormwater, reduce heat island effect, and connect development to existing infrastructure rather than sprawling into undeveloped land.

front: Surface-to-volume ratio and compact building form
back: A more compact building form has less exterior surface area relative to its enclosed volume, reducing heat loss and heat gain through the envelope and generally lowering heating and cooling energy use compared to a sprawling form.

front: Vegetative windbreak
back: A planted buffer of trees or shrubs positioned to block or redirect prevailing winter winds away from a building, reducing infiltration heat loss and improving outdoor comfort near entries and gathering spaces.

front: Low Impact Development (LID)
back: A stormwater management approach that mimics natural hydrology by managing rainfall close to where it falls, using strategies like bioswales, rain gardens, and permeable paving instead of routing all runoff to a single detention structure.

front: Permeable paving
back: Paving material or systems, such as porous asphalt or pervious concrete, that allow stormwater to infiltrate through the surface into the ground below, reducing runoff volume and supporting groundwater recharge.

front: Green roof
back: A roof system with a vegetated growing medium over a waterproofing and drainage layer, which reduces stormwater runoff, lowers roof surface temperature, provides insulation value, and can mitigate the urban heat island effect.

front: Bioswale
back: A shallow, vegetated channel designed to collect, slow, filter, and infiltrate stormwater runoff as it moves across a site, commonly used along parking areas and roadways as a low impact development strategy.

front: Orienting a site plan for daylighting quality
back: Positioning primary occupied spaces toward north and south exposures generally yields more even, glare-controlled daylight than east or west exposures, where low sun angles are harder to control without dedicated shading devices.

front: Solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC) and massing decisions
back: SHGC measures the fraction of solar radiation admitted through glazing. In massing and orientation decisions, a lower SHGC is typically favored on east and west facades to control unwanted heat gain, while south glazing can use a higher SHGC for passive heating.

front: Orienting building form relative to prevailing wind
back: In cold, windy climates a compact form with its narrow face and fewer openings turned toward prevailing winter winds reduces heat loss, while in hot humid climates orienting openings to capture prevailing breezes supports natural ventilation.

front: Xeriscaping
back: A landscaping approach using drought-tolerant, often native plant species and efficient irrigation to minimize water use, reducing a site's long-term water demand and maintenance compared to conventional turf-heavy landscaping.

front: Dark sky and light pollution considerations
back: Site lighting design that shields fixtures and directs light downward reduces glare, sky glow, and light trespass onto neighboring properties, an increasingly common contextual and sustainability consideration in site lighting layout.

front: What is occupancy classification and why does it matter in an initial code analysis?
back: Occupancy classification is the building code category assigned to a space based on its intended use, such as Assembly, Business, Educational, or Residential. It drives nearly every other code requirement, including allowable height and area, construction type, fire protection, and means of egress.

front: Type I construction (IBC)
back: The most fire-resistive construction type, built of noncombustible materials such as concrete and protected steel, with the highest fire-resistance ratings. It allows the greatest building heights and areas under the code.

front: Type V construction (IBC)
back: Construction in which structural elements, walls, and floors may be of any material permitted by code, including wood frame. It has the lowest fire-resistance rating and the most restrictive allowable height and area limits.

front: Types II, III, and IV construction (IBC), in general terms
back: Type II is noncombustible construction similar to Type I but with lower required fire-resistance ratings. Type III is exterior walls of noncombustible materials with any permitted interior construction. Type IV is heavy timber, now including mass timber types IV-A through IV-C.

front: How is a building's allowable floor area determined?
back: A base allowable area is set by occupancy classification and construction type, then increased for frontage on public ways or open space and further increased for automatic sprinkler protection, per the code's area formulas.

front: How is a building's allowable height determined?
back: Maximum allowable height and number of stories are set by tables that cross-reference occupancy classification against construction type. A more fire-resistive construction type generally permits a taller, larger building.

front: How do automatic sprinklers affect allowable building area and height?
back: Installing an automatic sprinkler system throughout a building typically allows an increase in allowable floor area and, in many occupancies, an increase in allowable height or number of stories above the unsprinklered base values.

front: How do the ADA Standards and ICC/ANSI A117.1 relate to each other?
back: The ADA Standards for Accessible Design are a federal civil rights requirement enforced nationwide, while ICC/ANSI A117.1 is a technical standard referenced by the building code. Many jurisdictions adopt A117.1 by reference, and its technical provisions are closely coordinated with the ADA Standards, though the two are not identical documents.

front: Accessible route
back: A continuous, unobstructed path connecting accessible building elements and spaces, usable by a person with a mobility disability, that includes walking surfaces, ramps, elevators, and accessible entrances.

front: Maximum running slope of an accessible route
back: 1:20, or 5 percent. A walking surface steeper than this threshold along its direction of travel is classified as a ramp and must meet ramp-specific requirements, including a maximum running slope of 1:12 (8.3 percent), landings, and handrails.

front: Maximum cross slope of an accessible route
back: 1:48, or about 2 percent, measured perpendicular to the direction of travel. This limit applies to walking surfaces, ramps, and accessible parking spaces and access aisles.

front: Minimum clear width of an accessible route
back: 36 inches along the route, though it may narrow to 32 inches at a point such as a doorway for a short distance. Wider clearances are required at passing spaces along a long narrow route.

front: Minimum clear opening width at an accessible doorway
back: 32 inches, measured between the face of the door and the stop, with the door open 90 degrees. This is the minimum clear passage width, not the nominal door leaf size.

front: How is the required number of accessible parking spaces determined?
back: It is set by a sliding scale table based on the total number of parking spaces provided in a lot, with the required percentage of accessible spaces decreasing as the total space count increases.

front: Van accessible parking space requirement
back: A portion of required accessible spaces must be van accessible, with either a wider parking space or a wider access aisle to accommodate a side loading wheelchair lift, plus additional vertical clearance for the vehicle.

front: Accessible turning space
back: A clear floor space allowing a wheelchair user to reverse direction, provided either as a 60 inch diameter circle or a T shaped space with specific arm dimensions, required in spaces such as accessible toilet rooms.

front: The three components of a means of egress
back: Exit access, the portion of the path leading to an exit, the exit itself, a protected path such as an enclosed stair, and exit discharge, the path from the exit to a public way.

front: How is occupant load calculated for a space?
back: The floor area of the space is divided by an occupancy load factor, in square feet per person, assigned by code based on the type of use, such as assembly, business, or storage. The result, rounded up, sets exiting and fixture requirements.

front: Why does occupant load factor vary so much by use?
back: The factor reflects how densely a space is typically occupied. A densely packed assembly space with fixed seating has a much smaller square foot per person factor than a low density use such as a warehouse or mechanical room.

front: What determines whether a space needs one exit or two or more?
back: The required number of exits is based primarily on occupant load and, for some occupancies, on common path of travel distance. Above a code specified occupant load threshold, at least two remote exits are required.

front: Common path of travel
back: The portion of exit access travel that occupants must traverse before two separate and distinct paths to two exits become available. It is limited by code to prevent a single point of failure trapping occupants.

front: Exit travel distance
back: The maximum distance an occupant may travel from any point in a space to reach an exit, measured along the natural path of travel. Limits vary by occupancy and are typically extended where the building is fully sprinklered.

front: Fire resistance rating
back: The time, in hours, that a building element such as a wall, floor, or column can withstand a standard fire exposure test while continuing to perform its structural or separation function.

front: Fire wall versus fire barrier
back: A fire wall provides structural stability to allow collapse of the structure on either side without the wall failing, effectively creating separate buildings. A fire barrier separates occupancies or areas within the same building but does not carry that structural independence requirement.

front: Purpose of the International Energy Conservation Code (IECC)
back: It sets minimum requirements for a building's thermal envelope, mechanical systems, lighting, and service water heating to reduce energy consumption, and it is the model energy code most US jurisdictions adopt in some form.

front: Building envelope requirements under an energy code
back: Minimum insulation values, or R-values, for walls, roofs, and floors, and maximum U-factors and solar heat gain coefficients for windows and doors, set to limit heat loss and gain through the building's exterior.

front: Prescriptive versus performance compliance path for energy codes
back: The prescriptive path requires meeting a fixed table of individual component values, such as insulation and glazing. The performance path allows trade offs between components as long as the whole building's modeled energy use meets or beats a baseline.

front: Separated versus non separated mixed occupancy
back: In a separated mixed occupancy, each occupancy is enclosed by fire barriers rated to code and each area is limited to its own allowable area. In a non separated mixed occupancy, no such separation is provided and the most restrictive code provisions of any occupancy present apply to the whole area.

front: Incidental use area
back: A subordinate space within a building, such as a boiler room or storage room, that presents a higher hazard than its surrounding occupancy and must be separated or protected per code, without being classified as its own distinct occupancy.

front: Typical building code trigger for high rise requirements
back: Most US model codes define a high rise as a building with an occupied floor located more than 75 feet above the lowest level of fire department vehicle access, triggering additional life safety requirements such as smoke control and fire service features.

front: Accessible toilet room clearance basics
back: An accessible toilet room needs a clear floor space for a turning maneuver, a water closet centered at a specified distance from the side wall with grab bars, and clear floor space at the lavatory, all coordinated with the accessible route into the room.

front: Why does exit width per occupant vary by occupancy in code egress calculations?
back: The code assigns a different width factor, in inches per occupant, to stairs versus level components, and assembly occupancies with concentrated crowds are held to different factors than lower hazard occupancies, reflecting differing evacuation dynamics.

front: How does a construction type fire resistance table work?
back: It cross references each building element, such as the structural frame, bearing walls, and floor or roof assemblies, against the construction type to specify the minimum required fire resistance rating in hours for that element.

front: Typical sequence of an initial code analysis
back: Determine occupancy classification, select or confirm construction type, check allowable height and area against the proposed building, and verify the means of egress system, before moving into more detailed fire protection and accessibility compliance.

front: ADA Title III program accessibility for existing buildings
back: Public accommodations must remove architectural barriers where readily achievable, and any alteration must make the altered portion accessible to the maximum extent feasible, even where a full retrofit of the entire existing building is not required.

front: What does zoning regulate, as distinct from the building code?
back: Zoning regulates land use, meaning what activities are permitted on a parcel, and bulk, meaning how large and how positioned a building may be, including height, setbacks, and floor area ratio. The building code regulates construction safety.

front: Setback
back: The minimum required distance between a building and a property line, typically specified separately for the front, side, and rear yards, within which no building may be constructed.

front: Floor area ratio (FAR)
back: The ratio of a building's total gross floor area to the area of the lot it sits on. A FAR of 2.0 on a 10,000 square foot lot allows up to 20,000 square feet of gross floor area.

front: How do you calculate maximum allowable gross floor area from FAR?
back: Multiply the FAR by the lot area. For example, a lot of 8,000 square feet with a zoning FAR of 1.5 permits a maximum of 12,000 square feet of gross floor area across all stories.

front: How is building height typically measured for a zoning height limit?
back: Height is usually measured from an established grade plane, often an average of the finished or natural grade around the building's perimeter, up to the highest point of the roof or a specified reference such as the mean height of a pitched roof.

front: Lot coverage
back: The percentage of a lot's area that may be covered by the building's footprint, distinguished from FAR, which measures total floor area across all stories rather than ground footprint alone.

front: Zoning parking requirement basis
back: Zoning ordinances typically require a minimum number of off street parking spaces per unit of use, such as spaces per dwelling unit or per thousand square feet of retail or office area, varying by use category.

front: Easement
back: A legal right allowing a party who does not own a parcel of land to use a defined portion of it for a specific purpose, such as utility access or a shared driveway, without transferring ownership of the land itself.

front: Common types of easements affecting a development site
back: Utility easements for underground or overhead lines, access easements for a shared driveway or path, and conservation easements that permanently restrict development to protect natural or scenic resources.

front: Variance
back: A limited waiver from a specific dimensional or use requirement of the zoning ordinance, granted by a zoning board of appeals when strict application of the ordinance would cause unnecessary hardship unique to the property.

front: Special exception, also called conditional use
back: A use explicitly listed in the zoning ordinance as permitted in a district only if it meets specific standards and receives approval, unlike a variance, which departs from the ordinance's stated requirements entirely.

front: Key distinction between a variance and a special exception
back: A variance departs from what the zoning ordinance otherwise requires and needs proof of hardship. A special exception is a use the ordinance already anticipates and permits, subject to meeting listed conditions, with no hardship showing required.

front: What must an applicant typically demonstrate to obtain a variance?
back: That the property has unique physical circumstances not shared by neighboring parcels, that strict application of the ordinance would deprive the owner of reasonable use of the land, and that granting relief will not harm the surrounding neighborhood or public interest.

front: Nonconforming use
back: A use of land or a building that was lawfully established before a zoning change but no longer complies with the current zoning ordinance. It is typically allowed to continue but is restricted from expanding and may lose its status if abandoned.

front: Zoning board of appeals
back: A local administrative body, separate from the planning or legislative board, that hears and decides applications for variances and special exceptions and reviews appeals of decisions made by a zoning administrator.

front: Site plan review
back: A local approval process, distinct from zoning permit issuance, in which a planning body reviews a proposed project's site layout, access, landscaping, and stormwater design against adopted design and engineering standards before construction can begin.

front: Overlay district
back: A zoning designation applied on top of an existing base zoning district that adds supplemental requirements, such as design standards, environmental protections, or historic preservation controls, without replacing the underlying district's base use and bulk rules.

front: Landscape buffer setback
back: An additional setback area, often planted with screening vegetation, required between differing land uses, such as a commercial property abutting a residential district, to reduce visual, noise, or light impacts on the neighboring use.

front: Density (residential)
back: A measure of development intensity expressed as dwelling units per acre, used by zoning ordinances to control the number of housing units permitted on a given parcel independent of building size or FAR.

front: Zoning map versus zoning ordinance text
back: The zoning map shows which district classification applies to each parcel in a jurisdiction. The zoning ordinance text sets out the actual use and dimensional standards, such as setbacks and FAR, that apply within each mapped district.

front: Rezoning versus a variance
back: Rezoning is a legislative act that changes a parcel's underlying zoning district classification, decided by the governing body such as a city council. A variance is a narrower administrative waiver of one or more specific standards within the existing district.

front: Planned unit development (PUD)
back: A zoning tool allowing a developer to propose a custom mix of uses, densities, and site layout for a larger tract, often trading design flexibility from standard district rules for public benefits such as open space or affordable units.

front: Frontage requirement
back: A zoning standard specifying the minimum width of a lot along a public street, ensuring adequate access and consistent street facing character within a district.

front: Building line versus lot line
back: The lot line is the legal boundary of the parcel. The building line is the setback line established by the zoning ordinance, located inside the lot line, beyond which no structure may be built toward the property boundary.

front: Accessory structure setback rules
back: Detached accessory structures such as sheds or garages are commonly permitted at reduced setbacks compared to the primary building, though they still must respect minimum distances from side and rear lot lines set by the ordinance.

front: Curb cut or driveway access approval
back: A separate permit, typically from the local public works or transportation department, authorizing a new opening in the curb or street frontage for vehicle access, reviewed for sight distance and traffic safety independent of zoning approval.

front: Right of way
back: A strip of land, often owned or controlled by a public agency, dedicated to a street, sidewalk, or utility corridor. Private setbacks are measured from the right of way line, which may sit inside the platted lot line.

front: Front, side, and rear yard
back: The front yard lies between the building and the street facing lot line, the side yards lie between the building and the side lot lines, and the rear yard lies between the building and the rear lot line, each governed by its own setback minimum.

front: Bulk plane or daylight plane
back: An angled setback plane, rising from a point above the side or rear lot line, that limits how far a building's upper stories may extend upward and outward, intended to preserve light and air to neighboring properties.

front: Zoning permit versus building permit
back: A zoning permit confirms a proposed use and building comply with the zoning ordinance's use and bulk standards. A building permit is a separate approval confirming compliance with the construction and life safety requirements of the building code.

front: Public hearing requirement for a variance
back: Most jurisdictions require published notice and a public hearing before the zoning board of appeals decides a variance application, giving neighboring property owners an opportunity to comment before a decision is made.

front: Use variance versus area (dimensional) variance
back: A use variance permits a land use otherwise prohibited in the district and is generally the hardest to obtain. An area variance permits a deviation from a dimensional standard, such as setback or height, while the use itself remains permitted.

front: Grandfathering of a nonconforming structure
back: A legally established structure that does not meet a current dimensional standard, such as a setback adopted after the structure was built, is typically permitted to remain as is, though repairs and any expansion may be restricted by the ordinance.

front: Sight triangle, or clear sight distance requirement
back: A zoning or engineering standard restricting the height of fences, walls, signs, and landscaping within a triangular area at a street corner or driveway intersection, to preserve a driver's line of sight for safety.

front: Impervious surface coverage limit
back: A zoning or stormwater ordinance standard capping the percentage of a lot that may be covered by impervious materials, such as building footprint and paving, to limit stormwater runoff and support groundwater recharge.

front: Wetlands, for regulatory purposes
back: Areas inundated or saturated by surface or groundwater at a frequency and duration sufficient to support vegetation adapted for saturated soil conditions, regulated primarily under the Clean Water Act's Section 404 permitting program.

front: Wetland buffer setback
back: A required no disturbance or limited disturbance zone measured outward from a delineated wetland boundary, imposed by a state, local, or federal agency to protect the wetland's ecological function from adjacent construction activity.

front: Floodplain
back: Land adjacent to a river, stream, or coastline that is subject to periodic inundation, mapped by FEMA and regulated to reduce flood damage risk and control development in flood prone areas.

front: 100 year floodplain and base flood elevation
back: The 100 year floodplain, or Special Flood Hazard Area, has a 1 percent annual chance of flooding. The base flood elevation is the computed elevation floodwater is expected to reach in that 1 percent annual chance event, used to set minimum finished floor elevations.

front: FIRM, or Flood Insurance Rate Map
back: The official map published by FEMA that delineates flood hazard zones, including the Special Flood Hazard Area and base flood elevations, used by local jurisdictions to administer floodplain regulations and by lenders to determine flood insurance requirements.

front: Floodway versus flood fringe
back: The floodway is the channel and adjacent area that must remain open to convey floodwater without significantly raising flood elevations, and new construction there is tightly restricted. The flood fringe is the remaining floodplain area outside the floodway, where development is permitted subject to elevation and floodproofing requirements.

front: Design requirement for structures in a Special Flood Hazard Area
back: The lowest floor of a new or substantially improved structure must generally be elevated to or above the base flood elevation, often with an added freeboard margin required by the local floodplain ordinance.

front: National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)
back: A federal program that makes flood insurance available to property owners in participating communities, in exchange for those communities adopting and enforcing floodplain management regulations that meet or exceed federal minimum standards.

front: When does historic preservation review typically apply to a project?
back: It applies when a property is individually listed or is a contributing structure within a designated historic district, whether at the local, state, or National Register level, and proposed exterior alterations, additions, or demolition are involved.

front: Section 106 review
back: A federal review process under the National Historic Preservation Act, triggered when a project involves federal funding, licensing, or approval, requiring the agency to assess the project's effect on historic properties before proceeding.

front: Local historic district commission or design review board
back: A local body that reviews proposed exterior changes to properties within a designated local historic district against adopted design guidelines, with authority to approve, deny, or condition the work before a building permit can be issued.

front: Certificate of Appropriateness
back: A local approval issued by a historic district commission confirming that a proposed exterior alteration, addition, or new construction within a historic district is consistent with the district's adopted design guidelines.

front: National Register of Historic Places listing, effect on private property
back: Listing alone imposes no restriction on a private owner's use of the property and does not require design review for work funded entirely privately, though it can trigger Section 106 review if federal funding or permits are involved and can qualify the property for historic tax credits.

front: Federal historic rehabilitation tax credit eligibility
back: A certified historic structure undergoing a certified rehabilitation may qualify for a federal tax credit, provided the work meets the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation, which emphasize retaining and repairing historic character defining features rather than replacing them.

front: Design overlay district
back: An overlay zoning designation that imposes supplemental architectural or site design standards, such as materials, massing, or streetscape requirements, on top of the base zoning district's use and bulk rules, often used to protect a neighborhood's visual character.

front: Environmental impact review, general concept
back: A regulatory process, required under federal law for major federal actions and under many state laws for state or local actions, requiring an analysis of a proposed project's significant environmental effects and consideration of alternatives before approval.

front: When is an archaeological survey typically required for a project?
back: When the project site has documented or probable potential to contain archaeological or cultural resources, often triggered as part of a Section 106 federal review or a state environmental review process for ground disturbing construction.

front: Coastal zone management regulation
back: State and local programs, often implemented under federal coastal management law, that regulate development along shorelines to protect coastal resources, control erosion, and manage public access, frequently requiring a separate coastal permit.

front: Steep slope ordinance
back: A local regulation restricting or adding requirements to development on land above a specified slope threshold, intended to reduce erosion, landslide risk, and stormwater runoff on hillside sites.

front: Tree preservation ordinance
back: A local regulation protecting designated trees, such as those above a specified trunk diameter or of a protected species, requiring a permit before removal and often mandating replacement planting or a protected root zone during construction.

front: Erosion and sediment control permit
back: A permit required before land disturbing construction activity, typically requiring a plan showing measures such as silt fencing and stabilized construction entrances to prevent sediment from leaving the site during construction.

front: Stormwater management requirement
back: A local or state requirement that new development control the rate and quality of stormwater runoff leaving a site, often through detention or retention facilities, to limit downstream flooding and pollutant discharge compared to pre development conditions.

front: Which agency typically issues wetland fill permits under federal law?
back: The US Army Corps of Engineers issues Section 404 permits for the discharge of dredged or fill material into wetlands and other waters of the United States, often in coordination with state environmental agencies.

front: Dry floodproofing versus elevation for nonresidential structures
back: Where local regulations allow, a nonresidential structure may be dry floodproofed, meaning it is made watertight below the base flood elevation, as an alternative to physically elevating the lowest floor, subject to certification by a licensed design professional.

front: How can a historic district and a floodplain or wetland regulation apply to the same site simultaneously?
